lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- The Person Who, the Thing That
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Gustavo Marinho de Carvalho | Lesson 9 -- The Person Who, the Thing That
phases: The Words of the Org Chart

listenings.text: When you start working with a company in another country, everybody hands you the same two things: the process and the calendar. Almost nobody hands you the third one, which is the only one you actually need in the first month. A map of the people. Not the org chart, which tells you the job titles, but the working map, which tells you who answers quickly and who does not, whose approval unblocks a thing and whose approval merely records it, and which of the four people copied on every email is the one who will read yours. Nobody writes that down, because everybody inside the company learned it by being there for two years. If you ask for it directly, in the first week, you will usually get it, and you will save yourself about six months.

There is a distinction I wish somebody had explained to me earlier, and it costs people a lot of time. The person you talk to and the person who decides are frequently not the same person, and in a lot of companies they are not even in the same conversation. Your point of contact may be perfectly senior, perfectly friendly and perfectly unable to approve what you are asking for. That is not a problem, and it is certainly not a reason to go around them, which never works and never goes unnoticed. It is simply information you need. The polite version of the question is short and nobody has ever taken offence at it. Who else needs to see this before it can move? Ask it early, ask it of the person you like, and write down the answer.
